summary: Absorption-cooked peppery red wine capellini: angel hair toasted 12 minutes at 375°F, then cooked in a single covered pot on top of zucchini, asparagus and tomatoes with red wine, smoked paprika, pepper and herbs, tossing every 3 minutes for 8-12 minutes; vegan, 30 minutes, serves 4.
glance: 1 pound capellini, broken into 3-inch lengths and toasted until golden
8-12 minutes covered, tossing every 3 minutes, with 1 1/4 cups red wine and 1 1/4 cups water
faq: What is absorption cooking for pasta?

Cooking pasta by adding a measured amount of liquid instead of boiling it in a gallon of salted water. It can be a big time saver: you don't wait for water to boil, and you may not need two pots if the sauce is built in with the pasta.
Why toast the noodles first?

Characteristic of how noodles are handled in Spain and Mexico (where they're called fideos) and the Middle East; the author enjoys the additional browned flavors. Do it while prepping and sauteing the vegetables.
How do I know when it's done?

Cook covered over medium heat and every 3 minutes remove the lid and toss; the total will be about 8 to 12 minutes. Taste a noodle toward the end, and if it's not done and there's no moisture left on the bottom add about 1/3 cup more wine or water.
Why less liquid than usual?
The tomatoes and zucchini cook along with the noodles and release liquid, so you check along the way and add more as needed.
Is it kid-friendly?
The flavor is quite assertive with substantial red wine, black pepper, smoked paprika and garlic, so the author wouldn't necessarily recommend it for young children or those who prefer milder tastes.

summary: Tofu dengaku: extra-firm tofu cut into 12 pieces, patted thoroughly dry and broiled on both sides (about 5 and 3 minutes), brushed with a red miso, mirin, sake and sugar glaze, returned to the broiler about 1 minute until bubbling, and skewered; vegan, 15 minutes, makes 12.
glance: rack at the top; about 5 minutes on the first side, about 3 on the second, then 1 minute glazed
2 tablespoons red miso, 1 tablespoon mirin, 1 tablespoon sake or sherry, 1 teaspoon sugar
faq: What is tofu dengaku?

Broiled tofu skewers, a street food in Japan grilled over wickedly hot charcoal. You can create a similar effect with your broiler, or use a grill for smoky flavor (oil the tofu well and put the skewers in first).
Why dry the tofu so thoroughly?

Use the firmest tofu you can find and dry the surface thoroughly: otherwise it keeps leaching out water and refuses to brown properly. Wrap the block in a dish towel, cut into 6 slabs then halve each, and pat the flat surfaces dry on both sides.
What does the miso glaze taste like?
If you only know miso in soup, it may be a surprise how it packs an almost chocolaty intensity when eaten practically straight.
How do I glaze it?
After both sides are browned, brush each piece with about 1 teaspoon of the sauce and return to the broiler until bubbling, about 1 minute.
Do I need skewers?
They're optional: 24 short wooden skewers (two per piece) are added afterwards so diners can pick them up. Finish with toasted sesame seeds.

summary: Seckel pears with cinnamon pastry crumbs, a deconstructed tart: tiny pears poached about 30 minutes in sugar and pear brandy, the liquid reduced to a caramel for crispy decorations, served on crumbled cinnamon shortbread crust with vanilla ice cream; serves 6 in 1 1/2 hours (20 active).
glance: 6 Seckel pears in 1 3/4 cups water, 1/2 cup sugar, 1/2 cup pear brandy, about 30 minutes
cinnamon pastry dough chilled at least 1 hour, rolled 1/8 inch, baked 375°F about 11 minutes, crumbled
faq: What are Seckel pears?

Pears that look like toys, about half the size of their larger brethren, with a brief season toward the end of fall. They're crisp like Boscs and fine to eat out of hand, but their size makes them even better for surprising desserts. If you can't find them, use larger pears cut in half.
Why is it a deconstructed tart?
A simple, cinnamon-spiked sandy crust is baked and then crumbled to serve as a base for a whole poached pear, with the poaching liquid simmered to a caramel for crispy decorations.
How do I make the caramel decorations?
After removing the pears, simmer the poaching liquid until it is a dark brown caramel, then drizzle it in thin lines on parchment or a silicone mat and let cool; you need only about 20 lines.
What do I do with the extra dough?

You can't practically make a smaller batch, so make more pears or bake extra as cookies: roll the dough into a 1 1/2-inch cylinder, wrap, refrigerate, slice and bake at 375°F until golden, about 15 minutes.
How do I serve it?
Place about 2 tablespoons of crumbs on each plate, make a hollow and rest a pear in it, add a small scoop of vanilla ice cream garnished with caramel lines, and give diners knives as well as spoons.

summary: Roasted maitake mushroom in smoky tea broth: 1 pound of maitake in four large pieces roasted about 20 minutes at 450°F, set in bowls with microwaved bok choy and a tamari-seasoned lapsang souchong tea broth steeped 5 minutes; vegan, 30 minutes, serves 4.
glance: 450°F (convection if available) about 20 minutes until fragrant, browning and tender
2 teaspoons lapsang souchong steeped 5 minutes in 2 cups boiling water, plus 1 tablespoon tamari
faq: What is maitake?

A mushroom very popular in Japan; in the US it's known as hen-of-the-woods (not to be confused with chicken-of-the-woods, which is completely different). Maitakes are rather expensive and unique, so the author makes them the focus of a dish.
What is lapsang souchong?
An intensely smoky tea unlike any other the author has had; its smokiness makes it a perfect broth base to show off the earthiness of roasted maitakes.
Why serve the mushroom in large pieces?
It's more dramatic when the maitake is in larger pieces, which also keeps it from getting soggy. Give guests a knife so they can cut the maitake at the last moment.
How should the broth taste?
Smoky, with a distinct note of soy and mildly salty: steep the tea, strain, add tamari, taste and add a bit of salt if needed. Reheat it in the microwave before serving.
How do I cook the bok choy?
Place the small-diced stems in a bowl with a tablespoon of water and microwave on high for one minute (or steam or blanch).

summary: Mexican breakfast torta: bolillo or telera rolls hollowed and toasted, layered with refried beans, scrambled eggs (or avocado for vegan), a broiled and peeled poblano, a lime-mayo red cabbage slaw, cotija and cilantro; a messy, good breakfast sandwich that serves 4.
glance: 4 bolillo or telera rolls (or a soft-interior American roll), some interior removed
2 cups refried beans, 6 scrambled eggs (or 1 avocado), roasted poblanos, cabbage slaw, cotija
Vegetarian; vegan option with avocado and no cheese
faq: What is a torta?

A Mexican sandwich, generally with a base of refried beans that can be topped with just about anything: here scrambled eggs (or avocado for a vegan version), a roasted poblano pepper and a simple cabbage slaw.
What rolls should I use?

The traditional rolls are bolillo or telera, available at a Mexican market. Or use an American sandwich roll with a thin crispy or soft crust but a light, soft interior that isn't hard to bite through. Remove some of the interior to make a trough that keeps the fillings in place.
How do I check vegetarian-ness?
Double-check the ingredients of the rolls and refried beans to make sure no lard is involved.
How do I prepare the poblanos?

Broil, turning every minute or so, until blackened and blistered all over, steam in a covered bowl 10 minutes, then peel, stem, halve and seed (rubber gloves help); it's okay if not every bit of skin comes off.
How do I serve it?
Wrapped in waxed paper or foil, or with a knife and fork, since these sandwiches are a messy good time; offer hot sauce at the table.

summary: Farro and chickpea soup: onion, celery, garlic and mustard greens softened, then 1 cup of farro simmered about 50 minutes in 4 cups of water (32 minutes at high pressure in a pressure cooker), finished with chickpeas and lemon juice; vegan, serves 4, 1 hour total (15 minutes active).
glance: 1 cup, simmered about 50 minutes or 32 minutes at high pressure
1 bunch mustard greens (or kale), stems removed, 1-inch ribbons
faq: Why farro in soup?

The author hasn't been fully sold on the farro revolution because its chewy texture becomes bothersome as a side dish or risotto-style, but in this soup it doesn't fall apart in the broth and makes the soup feel substantial, bordering on a stew that can be a one-pot meal.
Where does the farro come from?
The author used farro from ChefShop.com, grown in Eastern Washington by a family farmer, Lena Lentz Hardt, who escaped commodity wheat pricing by growing this organic grain.
Can I swap ingredients?

Use a different bean for the chickpeas (cannellini would be very Italian) or any kind of kale for the mustard greens. The author probably wouldn't use spinach, since its delicate texture might not hold up to the farro.
Can I use a pressure cooker?
Yes: cook the farro and 4 cups of water 32 minutes at high pressure followed by a quick pressure release, instead of simmering about 50 minutes covered until tender but still a bit chewy.
How do I finish it?
Add the chickpeas and lemon juice, simmer a few minutes to meld, and garnish with good olive oil, black pepper, parsley and flaky sea salt.

summary: Chanterelle banh mi bites: two-bite crostini of soft toasted baguette spread with sriracha mayo and topped with pickled daikon and carrot, cucumber, lemongrass-sauteed chanterelles, cilantro and jalapeno; 12 small crostini in 30 minutes (15 active), vegan with vegan mayonnaise.
glance: rice vinegar, sugar, salt, star anise; daikon and carrot chilled at least 20 minutes (up to 1 day)
12 small chanterelles fried 3 minutes with minced lemongrass
faq: What is banh mi?

Vietnamese sandwiches that have taken the West coast by storm: served on crusty baguettes, spread with a little mayo and stuffed with pickled vegetables and a filling of your choice. Tofu is usually on the menu, though vegetarians still have to watch out for fish sauce.
What can I use instead of chanterelles?
A thin slab of well-fried tofu, or portobello mushrooms cut into pieces that sit nicely atop the baguette slices.
How do I toast the baguette?
Toast the slices only very lightly: they should still be more soft than crunchy.
How do I make the quick pickle?

Cook the rice vinegar, sugar, salt, star anise and pepper over medium heat until nearly boiling and the sugar dissolves, turn off the heat, mix in the daikon rounds and julienned carrot, and refrigerate at least 20 minutes or up to a day.
How do I assemble them efficiently?

There are a lot of things on each crostini: do all of the mayo first, then all of the daikon, and so on. Each gets 1 teaspoon of mayo, a daikon slice, a cucumber slice, some carrots, a mushroom, cilantro, jalapeno and flaky salt.

summary: Basil gnudi with summer squash: ricotta dumplings (like gnocchi without potato) beaten with Parmesan, flour, a lot of basil and eggs, rolled in flour and simmered about 5 minutes until they rise, served in a white wine, garlic, summer squash and yellow cherry tomato saute with squash blossoms; serves 4 in 1 hour.
glance: 1 pound ricotta, 1/4 cup Parmesan, 6 tablespoons flour, 3/4 cup basil, 1 egg and 2 yolks
simmer about 5 minutes until they rise and stay up about 1 minute
faq: What are gnudi?

Like gnocchi made with ricotta instead of potato, or a ricotta ravioli filling without the pasta. At their best they are light and pillowy, and pair well with a delicate sauce that lets your handiwork with the dumplings shine.
How do I get the flour right?

The trick: enough flour to hold the dumplings together but not so much that they get heavy, which varies with the ricotta and eggs. Cook a test dumpling before shaping the rest, and if it falls apart stir in another tablespoon or so of flour.
What if my ricotta is watery?
Drain it with cheesecloth and a colander for a few hours. You don't need to if it is already fairly firm. The author calls Calabro by far the best widely available ricotta in the US.
Can I make them ahead?
Yes: form the gnudi (about 1 heaping tablespoon each, rolled in flour onto a floured baking sheet) and wrap and refrigerate them for a few hours before cooking.
Why basil?
The gnudi are flavored heavily with fresh basil; combined with the sweet dairy flavor of the ricotta and the tomatoes they're reminiscent of a Caprese salad and make a beautiful light entree.

summary: Red winter minestrone with winter greens pesto: a slowly caramelized sofrito (20-30 minutes) with leeks, carrot, turnips, beets, wine, green beans, white beans and their cooking liquid, served with a blanched-and-shocked pesto of beet greens, turnip greens and kale; vegan, serves 4 for dinner.
glance: 4 moderately as dinner with salad and bread
onion, tomato, garlic, herbs cooked at least 20-30 minutes into a caramelized base
3 cups bean cooking liquid plus 2 cups water (or 5 cups water)
beet and turnip greens plus kale, blanched and shocked, blended with olive oil, garlic and Parmigiano
faq: What is tip-to-tail greens pesto?

A pesto made from the greens of the beets and turnips plus kale. Blanch and shock the greens first: that removes a lot of the bitterness, so the result has a complex background flavor but lets the olive oil, Parmesan and garlic shine through. The recipe makes more than you need; use it on pasta, artisan toast or straight from a spoon.
Why is the soup red?
The soup gets its lovely red color from beets. In Italy minestrone can be made with just about any seasonal vegetables, and the author half-wants to call it borschtestrone.
Should I cook my own beans?
Highly recommended: the texture is better and you can use the bean cooking liquid as part of the broth for extra flavor (reserve 3 cups).
What is the sofrito and can I make extra?

Onions, tomatoes, garlic and herbs slowly cooked into a flavorful paste. If you have time, make a double or triple batch and save the rest for pasta, eggs or flavoring rice; sofrito freezes quite well.
How do I make the pesto ahead?
Reserve it in the refrigerator with plastic wrap pressed directly on the surface; each diner stirs a dollop into the soup.

summary: Real homefries: 1 1/2 pounds of skin-on diced potatoes fried in a single layer in a very big cast-iron skillet with onion and optional chile, flipped every 3 minutes until deep golden brown and crispy, served topped with flaky salt, and ideally with sunny-side-up eggs and garden tomatoes; vegan, 20 minutes.
glance: 2 as most of a meal or 4 as a side
1 1/2 pounds, any kind, skin on, 3/8-inch dice
single layer, flipping every 3 minutes, in 1/4 cup oil
yield: 2 as most of a meal or 4 as a side
faq: Why are homemade home fries better?

At home you can get them really browned and serve them while still crispy. In restaurants the potatoes are usually cut too large and cooked in a big pile on a flat-top griddle, where they mostly steam.
How do I get crispy home fries?

Use your biggest skillet, preferably cast iron, to maximize surface area. Fry the diced potato in a single layer (or as close as possible), flipping every 3 minutes or so with a spatula to get uncooked surfaces onto the skillet, until deep golden brown.
How should I cut the potatoes?
Into 3/8-inch dice, skin on; any kind of potato works.
How should I serve them?

Immediately, hot and crispy with flaky sea salt and pepper, as a whole meal with a couple of sunny-side-up eggs and, in late summer, thick slices of garden tomatoes; the yolk mixed with the potatoes and tomato juices is sublime.
Can I add heat?
Yes: saute a seeded, thinly sliced fresh chile de arbol or other hot pepper with the onion for 30 seconds before adding the potatoes.
